# From Glass to Skin: The Hidden Craft of a Sensor That Survives the Real World


August 31, 2026[Bo Chen VP, PC & Systems Engineering](https://www.synaptics.com/company/blog?author=Bo%20Chen) Share this article


*Part 5 of a series on Physical AI, tactile sensing, and the road to dexterous machines.*


For decades, the surface where humans met machines was built like glass: flat, rigid, sealed behind a screen, protected, and — when it finally cracked — replaceable. Nearly everything about how we built sensing surfaces assumed those properties.


A robotic fingertip inverts all of them.


The sensing surface of a robot's hand must be soft, not rigid. Curved, not flat. Exposed to the world, not sealed away. And most disorienting of all, it has to deform on purpose. A touchscreen is engineered to resist deformation, whereas a tactile fingertip embraces it. Deformation is how it senses force, shear, and contact. That inversion is the subject of this blog, and it's why a capable tactile sensor is far more than a clever chip.


## A tactile sensor is a stack, not a chip: inside robotic touch sensing


Cut a robotic fingertip in cross-section and you don't find a single component. You find a layered structure, each layer introducing materials and design decisions that affect the performance of the entire system.


At the surface sits a protective coating, the part that actually meets the world and absorbs the impact. Beneath it, a soft, elastomer skin compresses and shears under applied force. Below that, electrode layers read how the skin is deforming, with additional layers shaping the electrical fields along the way. A flexible substrate allows the structure to conform to a curved fingertip, with the sensing electronics integrated beneath it.


Every layer has to do its job, survive contact with the others, and keep doing both over time. Nothing downstream can help if the materials are wrong. The cleanest algorithm in the world can't reconstruct a signal that the physical stack never reliably captured in the first place.


## Why elastomer design matters in tactile sensing


The elastomer skin is the layer that surprises most people, because it's doing genuine mechanical work. It has to compress to register normal force pressing in, shear sideways to capture tangential force, and then return predictably to its original shape the instant the force is removed. It has to do all three repeatedly throughout the life of the sensor.


Tune the material too stiff and the fingertip goes numb — small forces become harder to detect. Tune it too soft and it never fully recovers; it lags, it holds a memory of the last grasp, it drifts and eventually tears. That lag is known as hysteresis, and it is widely regarded as the core materials challenge in soft tactile sensing.


Picture pressing your thumb into memory foam: when you lift off, the dent fills back in slowly rather than instantly. A robotic fingertip that behaves in the same manner is feeding its controller corrupt data, reporting a force that’s already changing or gone. In a fast manipulation task, that lag quietly destroys the real-time accuracy of the feedback loop.


Hysteresis is a solvable problem, not a wall. Materials science has made real progress on it, and that progress shows up everywhere downstream — in cleaner signals, tighter control loops, and more reliable grasps. The mechanical response of the skin — stiffness, recovery, how it's engineered to snap back — turns out to be as decisive as anything happening in the silicon.


It also feeds back into the signal problem from earlier in this series. A skin that deforms predictably produces a clean, interpretable signal. A skin that deforms erratically — that creeps, sticks, or changes with age — introduces variation that the rest of the sensing system then has to manage.


There is also a tradeoff between different sensing needs: a thicker, softer overlay improves compliance for sensing static pressure, but it also muffles higher-frequency vibrations useful for detecting slip. The skin’s thickness has to be tuned with both in mind. Mechanical design and signal quality are not separate problems. They're the same problem, viewed from two perspectives.


## Why robotic tactile sensors need to be thin and flexible


There's a constraint that quietly eliminates sensor approaches before the conversation even starts: thickness.


A human-scale robotic fingertip has limited space once tendons, actuators, wiring, and structural components are placed.


Thin electrode structures built on flexible substrates can conform closely to a fingertip and fill only a couple of millimeters or less of space. A camera-based optical sensor, by contrast, needs physical distance between its lens and the gel surface to focus, which pushes the fingertip depth toward fifteen to twenty-plus millimeters. That approach can produce rich data, but the additional package depth can become a system-level tradeoff in a dexterous hand. Once designers start instrumenting ten fingers, two palms, and more, thin, conformable sensing becomes an important structural advantage.


## From touch sensing to robotic tactile sensing


This is where a particular and slightly unglamorous history matters. Long before robotic fingertips, building touch and sensing systems for laptops, displays, and other devices required engineers to detect signals through and across different materials and thicknesses, while dealing with temperature, electrical noise, mechanical variation, and real-world use. Optimizing a sensing stack for system-level reliability, rather than for a single impressive number on a bench, is a discipline of its own.


That skill doesn't disappear when the application changes. The materials may be different, but the engineering judgment is familiar: balance sensitivity against robustness, signal quality against mechanical design, and performance against manufacturability.


## From tactile sensor research to manufacturable modules


There's a gap in robotics that doesn't get talked about enough: the distance between a tactile sensor that works in a research demonstration and one that can be built, by the thousand, into an actual robot hand.


Crossing that gap is its own engineering discipline — the discipline of the module. It means creating a structure that can be assembled consistently without hand-tuning every unit. It means designing for manufacturing yield. It means calibration that can be incorporated into production. And it means giving OEMs and ODMs a module they can integrate without having to solve every sensing, packaging, and materials problem again for themselves. None of this shows up in a sensitivity spec, and all of it determines whether a sensor can become a product.


Turning sensing concepts into manufacturable modules, at volume and with consistent performance, is the kind of engineering muscle built through decades of shipping touch modules at a planetary scale.


It is one of the less visible, but most important, parts of bringing tactile sensing into real machines.


## Designing robotic tactile sensors to survive real-world wear


A touchscreen lives a protected life. A robotic fingertip does not. It can be pressed, dragged, abraded, and compressed thousands of times a day against materials ranging from soft fabric to hard or irregular surfaces. A sensor that's accurate the day it's installed and unreliable a month later isn't a product; it's a liability, because a robot that thinks it can feel but can't is more dangerous than one that knows it's blind.


Designing the physical stack for longevity is therefore foundational. Protective coatings have to resist wear, elastomers have to retain predictable mechanical behavior through repeated cycles, adhesion between layers has to withstand fatigue, and calibration has to account for how the system ages. It's also one of the unsolved frontiers of the field, and we will return to challenges later in the series, including drift, wear, hysteresis, and the durability questions that separate an impressive tactile demonstration from a sensing system that can be deployed reliably.


For now, the point is this. A tactile fingertip is a physical object first: a small, layered, deforming structure that has to survive the world while reporting on it faithfully. But a faithful physical signal is only half of touch. Once the skin has captured what's happening, something has to interpret that signal instantly, right there on the hand, before the rest of the robot.


That's the brain. And that's where we go next.


*Next in the series: **The Brains in Your Fingertips** — how intelligence at the edge turns raw contact into meaning, finger by finger, and fuses a whole hand into a single sense.*
